near_miss.lead: Giving a weapon to a guest or follower
near_miss.why_not: Norse gaf ... brand and Homeric δώσω ... ἄκοντα share gift context but neither the gift verb nor the weapon designation supplies an exact cognate pair. Ordinary elite gift exchange is insufficient to reconstruct wording.

near_miss.lead: Hearing words; conveying words to ears
near_miss.why_not: Norse hearing an embassy and Greek hearing a continuous address are compatible speech situations, but the Greek passage lacks the ears expression. No distinctive shared construction beyond ordinary speech and hearing.

Norse kne is kné, knee/lap, after i, with the placing of the supplicant’s head in the preceding context. The assigned Greek passage concerns mutilation of herms, not supplication. Corpus search finds Homeric knee grasping, recorded separately as a search lead; its verb and gesture differ.

near_miss.lead: Passing words from man to man
near_miss.why_not: maðr is nominative singular and manne dative singular of maðr, creating distributive polyptoton in an injunction to transmit the king’s warning. The assigned Greek passage gives military orders without that figure. Searches for man/word roots, including non-Menota material and Sanskrit manuṣya/vac, yielded no matching cross-branch transmission formula in inspected hits; most were generic or Christian speech contexts.

Norse fætr (fótr, plural) and gengit (ganga, participle) describe the traveller’s feet; Vedic padbhiḥ is instrumental and gacchataḥ has the ox and ploughman as its subjects. The marked Norse old-path phrase is absent. Searches returned mundane walking-on-foot examples in Sanskrit epic and Christian Germanic texts. Cognate feet alone and predictable motion vocabulary do not establish a formula.

near_miss.lead: Night and day as a temporal totality
near_miss.why_not: The closest slab match is nótt oc dag against Herodotus 5.23.2 ἡμέρης καὶ νυκτός. Night is cognate; day is lexically different, order and case construction differ. Searches found numerous Greek combinations, including personifications and simple chronological contrasts. Continuous travel, attendance, meetings, and prospective obedience offer no distinctive shared poetic or ritual context; this readily independent merism is insufficient.

near_miss.lead: Sleeping or staying through the night
near_miss.why_not: The Norse narrative gives ordinary lodging, sleep and morning events; Homer’s ἀΰπνους νύκτας ἴαυον emphasizes sleepless nights. No matching marked epithet or inherited verb pair, and the shared night word is predictable.

Norse fell til fota describes surrender/supplication, absent from either assigned Greek partner. Inspected Homeric foot/fall search hits concern combat or childbirth. A Josephus supplication parallel was found separately, but biblical narrative and a conventional gesture cannot establish inherited wording; recorded as a search lead with this limitation.

Norse móðir mín er systir hans identifies the speaker’s mother as Erling’s sister. Irish siair do máthar is sister (oblique singular of siur) governed by co, with máthar genitive singular of máthair: the addressee’s maternal aunt. Cognate kin terms, but reversed relation and different syntax; ordinary genealogy, not a distinctive inherited phrase.

Norse binda takes sætt in following context, metaphorically concluding a settlement. Sanskrit badhnantaḥ takes setuṃ, constructing a bridge. The bind verbs are cognate but the object and action are not. The inspected bandha search hits concern literal bonds or release; none corroborates a shared settlement formula.

error.correct_reading: fœri/føri, preterite subjunctive singular of fara
error.evidence: The literal ogon; string is damaged character/entity encoding. The earl asks why the man should behave/go thus; this is an inflected verb, not the supplied unknown token.

error.correct_reading: hann stað, two words: pronoun hann and accusative singular stað of staðr
error.evidence: nam ... stað is the construction for stopping; the subject pronoun has been fused to the object noun.

error.correct_reading: Hundi, personal name; mark as name in this passage
error.evidence: Explicit naming after son ... er hét, followed by a statement that Hundi remained with Óláfr. It is not an ordinary dog noun here.

error.correct_reading: Hvelpr, alternative personal name/byname; mark as name
error.evidence: The naming construction gives Hundi eða Hvelpr as alternatives for the same hostage son. The animal-derived name is not independent evidence for womb phraseology.

error.correct_reading: rǫðu/ræðu, accusative singular of ræða, speech/conversation
error.evidence: Damaged ogon; entity occurs in the object of sagðe with alla, referring to the conversation with the king. Exact manuscript vowel should be checked against the edition; the literal entity debris is certainly not linguistic text.

given_etymon.gloss: root: to resound; ringing, whistling; to speak loudly, to proclaim

error.evidence: Dependent on ván and agreeing with slicra: expectation of such answers. It is not the infinitive of svara in this syntax; historical relation between noun and verb does not fix the lemma error.
The king addresses Sveinn and the following subject Sveinn casts aside his cloak and knife. This is not the common noun boy/servant or a reflexive-pronoun occurrence.

given_etymon.gloss: to seek out, give a sign, track

error.evidence: The verse’s travel context and the adjacent variant sottum support a finite verb, not the noun sótt, illness. Variant readings should not be treated as multiple independent tokens.

search_lead.cognate: Norse kné (slab kne) and Greek γόνυ (γούνων) continue the inherited knee noun. No cognacy is asserted between the gesture verbs.
search_lead.argument: Both locate a request for protection or favour at the superior’s knees. Norse places the head in the earl’s lap/knee; Homer has Thetis grasp Zeus’s knees. This is a comparison of supplication gestures for further review, not evidence of an exact inherited phrase; the shared body part and different gestures may arise independently. The appropriate Greek passages are outside the slab.

search_lead.cognate: Norse fótr (fota) and Greek πούς (πόδας) are cognate; no cognacy is asserted for the falling verbs.
search_lead.argument: A subordinate falls before a king and appeals to his power of mercy in both narratives. Josephus additionally describes grasping the feet. This late biblical witness is excluded-layer material and may explain a widespread or transmitted supplication convention rather than PIE phraseology; the Norse scene also explicitly invokes God. No inheritance claim is warranted.

note: Read all 212 bundles in order in sections 1–25, 26–65, 66–110, 111–155, 156–190, 191–212; revisited promising passages with context and word metadata. Corpus queries tested knee/foot supplication, speech transmission, walking, night/day, and binding. No defensible inherited-phrase claims. 10 near-misses, 2 search leads, 8 error reports.
